cards.explanation: The answer is children. Jacob looks up, sees Esau coming with four hundred men, and divides the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). Leah and Rachel are Jacob's wives. The text shows him sorting the children and doesn't say why. I can't even sort a cookie box without a mess, so I'm impressed.

The answer is Rachel, Jacob's wife. She and her son Joseph are at the rear (Genesis 33:2). The maidservants and their children go in front, and Leah and her children come next. The text doesn't say why Jacob lined them up this way, so I'll leave that one alone.

The answer is out ahead of them all. Jacob himself goes on ahead of his whole family (Genesis 33:3). Four hundred men are walking up, and he's the first one they'll meet. That takes nerve, friends, and I think it took every bit of it.

The answer is True. Esau ran to him, embraced him, threw his arms around his neck and kissed him (Genesis 33:4). Jacob had bowed to the ground seven times as he approached (Genesis 33:3), and Esau ran to him anyway. I did NOT have that on my bingo card.

The answer is that God graciously gave them to him. Jacob tells Esau, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant." (Genesis 33:5). He doesn't brag about them. He points to God's grace. And notice he calls himself Esau's servant.

The answer is "To find favor in your sight." Jacob says, "To find favor in your sight, my lord…" (Genesis 33:8). Esau came with four hundred men, and Jacob calls him "my lord" and asks for his favor. I've handed over a warm cookie to win somebody over, but this is a whole company. I think it's a humble way to walk up to his brother, friends.

The answer is False. Esau says, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you" (Genesis 33:9). Jacob has to press him before he finally accepts (Genesis 33:11). Two brothers, each insisting the other keep the goods. That's a polite standoff, friends.

The answer is True. Jacob says, "…I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably." (Genesis 33:10). The reason is in his own words: Esau received him favorably. Earlier, Jacob was greatly afraid when he heard Esau was coming with four hundred men (Genesis 32:6-7). I think that's why this welcome lands so hard.

The answer is that his children are frail and his herds are nursing. Jacob says the children are frail and he must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young. He adds that if they are driven hard for even a day, all the animals will die (Genesis 33:13). That's the reason he gives for asking Esau to go ahead. A good dad knows his crew's speed.

The answer is Seir. Jacob says he'll come along slowly "…until I come to my lord at Seir." (Genesis 33:14). Seir is the place Esau heads back to (Genesis 33:16). Jacob's promise sounds friendly, and the text then shows him going to Succoth (Genesis 33:17).

The answer is False. Esau says, "Let me leave some of my people with you…" and Jacob answers, "Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord." (Genesis 33:15). He doesn't take the offer. Esau leaves for Seir that same day (Genesis 33:16).

The answer is a house. At Succoth, Jacob built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock, and that is why the place was called Succoth (Genesis 33:17). I spent years behind a pile of old takeout menus in a junk drawer, so a roof and four walls sound pretty fancy to me, friends.

The answer is Succoth. Jacob built shelters for his livestock there, "that is why the place was called Succoth." (Genesis 33:17). The name comes from what he built. A whole place named after livestock shelters, friends.

The answer is True. Jacob camps just outside Shechem, and the plot where he pitched his tent he purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father (Genesis 33:18-19). He paid a hundred pieces of silver for it (Genesis 33:19). He didn't just park and hope. He paid for his spot.
The answer is an altar. There Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:20). He buys the land, then sets up an altar on it. I think that tells you what mattered to him.
